title: The Lake That Stole the Air — Lake Nyos (1986)
sources: US Geological Survey (USGS Open-File Report 87-97): 'The 21 August 1986 Lake Nyos Gas Disaster, Cameroon' by George W. Kling et al. — https://pubs.usgs.gov/of/1987/0097/report.pdf (at least 1,700 people killed; magmatic CO2 accumulated in deep cold bottom waters; exact triggering mechanism undetermined; no direct volcanic eruption)

NASA Earth Science: 'Lake Nyos, Cameroon' — https://science.nasa.gov/earth-science/programs/research-analysis/lake-nyos-cameroon/ (limnic eruption / lake overturn; dense CO2 cloud flowed down valleys displacing breathable air)

lines.text: A lake killed at least seventeen hundred people in a single night.
lines.caps: A *lake killed | at least *1,700 people | in a single *night.

lines.text: On August twenty-first, nineteen eighty-six, at Lake Nyos in Cameroon,
a massive cloud of carbon dioxide suddenly burst from the deep crater lake.
lines.caps: a cloud of *carbon dioxide | suddenly *burst | from the deep *lake.

lines.text: Heavier than air, an almost invisible carbon dioxide cloud spread through the valleys,
flowing downhill, where high concentrations displaced oxygen and caused asphyxiation.
For decades, volcanic gas from deep underground had seeped into the cold bottom water,
trapped under immense pressure like a giant sealed bottle.
Investigators found no lava, no ash, and no conventional volcanic eruption,
lines.caps: Investigators *found | no lava or *ash, | no volcanic *eruption,

lines.text: and the exact trigger remained undetermined.
Scientists called this rare phenomenon a limnic eruption:
the night a quiet lake overturned and stole the air.
lines.caps: the night a *lake | *overturned and | stole the *air.
